title: Shared jeeps of the hills: stands, seats and fares
meta_description: How shared jeeps work in Siliguri, Darjeeling and Kalimpong: where the stands are, how to buy a seat, which seat to ask for, and indicative fares for 2026.
summary: Shared jeeps are how the hills travel: ten seats, a fixed fare per seat, and a departure when the vehicle fills. From Siliguri a seat to Darjeeling costs about ₹250–350 and to Kalimpong about ₹200–300. Buy at the counter, ask for a seat number, go in the morning, and keep luggage light.
key_takeaways: Shared jeeps sell individual seats at fixed fares from counters at each town's stand, and leave when all ten or so seats are sold.
In Siliguri, Darjeeling jeeps leave from around the central bus terminus and Gangtok and Kalimpong jeeps from the SNT and Panitanki More area.
Morning is the time to travel: most departures from the hill towns thin out by early afternoon, and the last jeep may leave before 4 pm.
If you want space or the front seat, buy two seats or ask for seat numbers one and two the day before at the counter.

sections.heading: How a shared jeep works
paras: Almost every hill road in this region is served by shared jeeps: Tata Sumos, Mahindra Boleros and similar four-wheel-drive vehicles that carry about ten people. Two or three sit in front beside the driver, four in the middle row and four on the side-facing benches or rear seat at the back. Each seat has a fixed fare, set by the local drivers' association for that route, and you pay only for your seat. The jeep leaves when it is full, not to a timetable.

Tickets are sold at small counters, often a wooden booth or a desk with a ledger, at each town's stand. The clerk writes your name and seat number, and on busy routes you can book a seat a day ahead. Luggage goes on the roof under a tarpaulin, tied down by the driver or a helper; a small daypack can stay on your lap. On most routes nobody haggles over a seat fare. You pay what the board or the clerk says.

For families of four or five, a reserved car can cost not much more than a stack of seats, and you choose when to leave. For solo travellers, couples and students, shared jeeps cut transport costs to a fraction, and they are how most local people travel.

sections.heading: The Siliguri stands
paras: Siliguri, at the foot of the hills, is where most trips begin, and it has several stands rather than one. Jeeps to Darjeeling, Kurseong and Mirik gather along Hill Cart Road around the Tenzing Norgay Central Bus Terminus. Jeeps and taxis for Gangtok and Kalimpong leave from the SNT terminus, the Sikkim government bus station further along Hill Cart Road, and from the Panitanki More area nearby. Ask an auto driver for the stand by the destination name and you will usually be dropped at the right counter.

There are also jeeps waiting outside New Jalpaiguri (NJP) station, mostly for Darjeeling and Gangtok, at much the same fares. They are handy when you step off an overnight train, though touts can be pushy; ask for the seat fare first and confirm whether the vehicle is shared or reserved. From Bagdogra airport there are no shared jeeps straight to the hills, so most people take a taxi to Siliguri, about ₹400–600, and pick up a seat there.

sections.heading: Darjeeling and Kalimpong stands
paras: In Darjeeling the main motor stand sits below Chowk Bazaar, a crowded strip of counters and vehicles reached by steep lanes from the Mall and Laden La Road. Separate counters sell seats for Siliguri and NJP, Kurseong, Mirik, Kalimpong and Gangtok; jeeps for Ghum, Sukhia Pokhari and nearby villages leave from the same area. Walk down early, find the counter for your destination, and ask for a seat number. The stand is busiest from about 6 to 10 am.

Kalimpong's Motor Stand is in the middle of town, a short walk from the main bazaar. It sends jeeps down to Siliguri, across to Gangtok and Darjeeling, and out to the villages: Lava, Pedong, Lolegaon, Rishyap and Algarah among them. The village routes have fewer departures, mostly in the morning, and some run only once or twice a day. If you are heading to a homestay village, ask your host which jeep they use and when it leaves; hosts often know the driver by name and can hold a seat for you.

sections.heading: What a seat costs: indicative fares
paras: Fares below are per seat on a shared jeep and per vehicle for a reserved small car, as we understand them for 2025–26. They move with fuel prices and season, and festival weeks can add a little. Treat them as a guide and check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Which seat to ask for
paras: Seat numbers matter on a three-hour mountain road. The front seats beside the driver have the best view, the most legroom and the least motion, and they sell first; locals and regular travellers book them a day ahead. The middle row is a fair compromise. The rear benches are the cheapest place to be only in the sense that everyone pays the same; they bounce the most, have the least air and the worst view, and are where motion sickness starts.

If you get carsick, ask for a front or window seat, eat lightly before you leave, and keep a window open. If you are travelling as a couple and want room, buying three seats in a row of four is a common and accepted practice; the counter will simply sell you the extra seat. Families sometimes buy the whole middle row.
list: Book the front seat a day ahead on busy routes.
Carry small notes; counters often lack change for ₹500.
Keep a jacket and water inside, not on the roof.
Note the vehicle number on your ticket before you walk away.

sections.heading: On the road: stops, courtesy and changes
paras: A shared jeep is a small community for three hours, and a few habits make it easier for everyone. Be at the stand ten minutes before the jeep is due to fill, because a full jeep does not wait for a ticket holder who has wandered off for tea. Hand your bag to the helper for the roof rather than climbing up yourself, and point out anything fragile.

On the long routes the driver stops once, usually at a roadside tea stall about halfway: Rohini or Kurseong on the way to Darjeeling, a Teesta-side bazaar or a ridge village on the Kalimpong and Gangtok runs. It is a ten- to fifteen-minute halt for tea, momos and the toilet, and it is the only one, so use it. Drivers also drop and pick up people along the road; if you want to get off before the final stand, tell the driver when you board and again as you get close.

Smoking inside is not acceptable, and most drivers will not play music loudly if you ask politely. Keep your phone conversations short, and if someone older or unwell needs the front seat, offering yours is common courtesy here. If you need to change jeeps, at Kurseong or Ghum for example, you buy a fresh seat at the next stand; through tickets are rare.

sections.heading: Timing, seasons and the roads
paras: Shared jeeps run from early morning, often from 6 am, and leave as they fill. From the hill towns the steady flow down to Siliguri slows by early afternoon, and the last departure may be at 3 or 4 pm, earlier in winter. Coming up from Siliguri, a jeep can usually be found until mid-afternoon on the main routes. Village routes are thinner still: plan on a morning jeep, and if you miss it, budget for a reserved car.

In October, the Puja holidays, late December and May–June, seats on the Darjeeling, Kalimpong and Gangtok routes sell out early, and booking the evening before is wise. In the monsoon, from June to September, landslides close roads for hours or days, and jeeps detour or wait. NH10 along the Teesta, the main road between Siliguri, Kalimpong and Gangtok, has had long closures and damage since the October 2023 flood; jeeps have used longer routes by way of Lava or Pedong on some days. Check current status before you travel, and leave slack in your plans.

faqs.q: How much is a shared jeep from Siliguri to Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About ₹250–350 a seat, with the journey taking 3–3.5 hours on a normal day. Jeeps leave from the stands along Hill Cart Road near the Tenzing Norgay Central Bus Terminus and from outside NJP station. Fares rise a little in peak weeks and when fuel prices change, so check current status before you travel and confirm the fare at the counter.

faqs.q: Can I book a shared jeep seat in advance?
faqs.a: Yes, at the counter at the stand, usually from the evening before. The clerk writes your name and seat number in a ledger or on a slip. This matters most for the front seats and in peak weeks such as October, the Puja holidays and late December. A few routes also take phone bookings through hotels or homestays, but there is no single online system for shared jeeps.

faqs.q: Where is the Kalimpong shared jeep stand?
faqs.a: Kalimpong's Motor Stand is in the centre of town, near the main bazaar. Counters there sell seats to Siliguri, Gangtok and Darjeeling, and to villages such as Lava, Pedong, Lolegaon and Rishyap. Village jeeps leave mainly in the morning and some run only once or twice a day, so ask the counter or your homestay host about timings the day before.

faqs.q: Is a shared jeep safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Shared jeeps are an everyday way for local women, students and families to travel, and solo women use them widely. Travel by day, choose a front or middle seat, and note the vehicle number on your ticket. Avoid the last jeep of the day if you can. If anything feels wrong, ask to be dropped at the next town stand and take another vehicle.

faqs.q: What happens to shared jeeps when roads are closed by landslides?
faqs.a: Jeeps wait, turn back or take a longer road. On the Kalimpong and Gangtok routes, closures of NH10 along the Teesta since the October 2023 flood have pushed traffic onto longer roads at times, adding hours and sometimes raising fares. In the monsoon, from June to September, keep a buffer day and check current status before you travel with the counter or your host.
